column3: Near-verbatim continuation: affluent speakers claim their fathers' community and follow its tracks.
It directly prefers what was found among the fathers over what God sent down.
Preference for worldly life does not address ancestral authority or claimed guidance.
The people defend their worship solely by finding their fathers doing it.
The preceding verse asks whether any prior book authorizes their inherited practice.
It gives a positive criterion for following rightly guided messengers.
The people justify devotion to idols by finding their fathers worshipping them.
The immediate continuation tests whether a messenger brings better guidance than the fathers' way.
Later generations rush along the tracks left by their fathers.
Moses is rejected as one who would turn people from the way found among their fathers.
Fear of God and the Hour does not illuminate inherited following.
It defines genuine guidance through faith unmingled with wrongdoing.
Ancestral custom is falsely presented as divinely commanded and is denied that warrant.
It invokes earlier messengers to reject worship other than God, challenging inherited polytheism.
God's unopposed guidance broadly contrasts with their self-ascribed guidance.
Its finding of a broken covenant concerns neither ancestors nor a claimed path.
The next verse gives the consequence for the deniers described in the immediate passage.
Following the Messenger is presented as the route to guidance.
Its reference to traces means grief after those who reject the message, not inherited tracks.
Within the surah, both the people and their fathers receive respite until truth and a messenger arrive.
Refusal of God's signs results in lack of guidance, countering their claim to be guided.
Those diverted from the path think themselves guided, directly exposing false self-assessment.
The demand to restore ancestors concerns resurrection, not following them.
Guidance is tested by recognizing a transformed throne, not by ancestral allegiance.
It depicts legitimate succession in the footsteps of messengers and revealed scripture.
Abraham names the Creator as the one who will guide him, opposing inherited idol worship.
Following Moses' tracks is shown within a later failure, warning that proximity to a leader is insufficient.
It identifies a repeated ancestral pattern of saying what earlier people said.
Abraham questions the idols to which his father and people remain devoted.
Moses offers Pharaoh guidance toward his Lord, a direct alternative to entrenched authority.
The brothers' appeal to their father is unrelated to religious following.
The same surah recounts Moses' mission to Pharaoh but does not invoke ancestral practice.
The Book is identified as the genuine source of guidance, unlike an untested inherited track.
A single community under one Lord only loosely contrasts with inherited communal identity.
Abraham explicitly declares both the people and their fathers to be in manifest error.
It calls to the Lord's path and distinguishes those astray from the rightly guided.
The command to worship one Lord provides only a broad contrast to inherited worship.
The same surah establishes a history of prophets sent among earlier peoples.
False intermediaries are defended as a route to God, an indirect parallel to unauthorized religion.
Jesus follows prior revelation and confirms it, distinguishing revelation-based continuity from imitation.
God's lordship over creation does not address the claimed ancestral path.
Calling the revelation inherited magic does not concern following ancestral guidance.
Those taking devils as patrons believe themselves guided while they are astray.
The same surah reports that earlier peoples mocked every prophet who came to them.
It commands following the guidance God gave the prophets, supplying the valid model of imitation.
The later admission of wrongdoing gives a consequence but not the ancestral rationale.
God is also the Lord of the earliest fathers, a limited corrective to ancestral authority.
It attributes guidance to God rather than to a community's own self-description.
The leaders' dismissal of Hud parallels rejection of a messenger without ancestral language.
The people make a conditional claim that they will be guided within the surah's Pharaoh narrative.
It compares the relative rightness of paths without addressing inherited authority.
Abraham replaces the fathers' worship framework with the Creator's lordship.
The admission of wrongdoing at punishment does not clarify ancestral following.
It identifies God's revealed Book as guidance, but has no ancestral contrast.
Earlier peoples reject messengers and doubt the summons, extending the repeated resistance pattern.
The drowning of Pharaoh's people is a distant narrative consequence without the focus mechanism.
Inherited sectarian claims to guidance are answered with Abraham's uncompromised way.
Preservation of the Reminder supplies a textual warrant but no direct ancestral contrast.
Questioning messengers and their peoples concerns accountability rather than inherited practice.
A people knowingly turn from their messenger, and their deviation is answered by loss of guidance.
Continued warning of a doomed people is only a general messenger-response parallel.
Jesus is described as a favored servant and example, not as an ancestral authority.
Choosing error over guidance gives a broad contrast to their claim of being guided.
It states that every community has received a warner, framing the repeated ancestral response.
Travel through secure towns is unrelated to religious tracks or guidance.
Belief leads God to guide the heart, but the verse has no social-inheritance dimension.
The denial of belief in a blame dialogue does not address ancestral following.
God's dominion and knowledge of the Hour do not clarify the focus claim.
It makes following God's guidance the explicit alternative to inherited custom.
It closely repeats the command to follow revelation and the reply that ancestral practice suffices.
The punishment of wrongdoers does not identify their source of guidance.
Physical paths enabling guidance offer only a lexical and broad thematic contrast.
Followers admit that obedience to their leaders led them away from the path.
Turning from the Merciful's reminder results in a devilish companion, explaining false guidance in the surah.
Personal responsibility for remaining guided only broadly contrasts with collective imitation.
It explicitly says that the fathers they found were astray.
It commands following the messenger on a straight path, the same surah's direct corrective.
Guidance or error is assigned to the hearer's own response to Qur'anic recitation.
It directly rejects the summons to God and the Messenger in favor of what fathers were found upon.
The people's objection to the example of Jesus does not address ancestral following.
The Qur'an is called guidance, broadly contrasting with refusal of revealed direction.
The brothers' plan to persuade their father is unrelated to religious authority.
Signs and affliction aim to make Pharaoh's people return, but not through an ancestral-track theme.
The two paths establish a general account of offered guidance.
Finding a possession and judicial restraint have no connection to ancestral custom.
The critique of attributing daughters to God does not clarify inherited following.
It attributes guidance solely to God in a distinct charitable context.
The mention of a father is familial, not an appeal to ancestral practice.
The Qur'an's place in the Mother of the Book provides only a remote textual-authority contrast.
Messengers follow the paths God showed them despite opposition, a positive model against inherited paths.
The claim that the Merciful has a child does not involve following fathers or tracks.
Ancestors and descendants may be chosen and guided to a straight path by God, not by lineage alone.
Changing a commanded word concerns disobedience, not ancestral guidance.
Future guidance and restored condition for martyrs has no connection to inherited authority.
The Messenger's lack of requested payment is unrelated to the focus claim.
Possessing scripture without carrying it out critiques inherited religious status without lived guidance.
Truth does not follow people's desires, contrasting a standard tested by revelation with inherited preference.
People reject guidance because a human messenger violates their assumed model, an analogous untested standard.
Selective hearing and altered words show corrupted religious authority, without an ancestral claim.
The record of people's traces concerns enduring effects, not following ancestors' tracks.
Abraham challenges his father's adoption of idols, providing a close familial-authority contrast.
Polytheists invoke both God's will and their fathers' practice to defend association without knowledge.
Exclusive worship is rejected because it would require leaving what the fathers worshipped.
Inherited names for alleged deities are denied any authority sent down by God.
Descendants name their fathers' prior association, directly exposing inherited religious liability.
Salih's people reject his call because it would require abandoning what their fathers worshipped.
Shu'ayb's people frame his message as a demand to abandon what their fathers worshipped.
Joseph follows the faith of his fathers while explicitly rejecting association, distinguishing valid continuity.
Associators appeal to divine will and their fathers' practice instead of accepting the messengers' warning.
It forbids following what one has no knowledge of, directly testing an unexamined inherited track.
Abraham warns his father that worship can amount to following Satan rather than the Merciful.
The leaders reject the messenger because he calls them away from what their fathers worshipped.
Abraham confronts the objects worshipped by both his people and their ancient fathers.
It forbids obeying parents in association and commands following the path of those who turn to God.
Opponents dismiss the message as unheard among their forefathers and defend inherited religious precedent.
The leaders reject the call because they have not heard it in the latter inherited religion.
Abraham disavows what his father and people worship, setting up the passage's contrast to inherited tracks.
Abraham leaves a lasting word among his descendants, contrasting examined transmission with blind imitation.
The challenge asks for a prior book or trace of knowledge, reinforcing the demand for warrant over inheritance.
Names assigned by people and their fathers lack divine authority, while guidance has come from the Lord.
Noah's people are urged by their leaders not to abandon their established gods, preserving inherited worship.
Jacob's children affirm worship of the one God worshipped by their fathers, showing a valid inherited monotheism.
Believers are forbidden to take fathers or brothers as allies when they prefer disbelief to faith.
Their worship is explicitly described as a repetition of what their fathers worshipped before them.
